fields.title: Group generation: separate ideation from evaluation
fields.keyTakeaway: Ideas and criticism cannot coexist in the same room at the same time. As soon as someone says “that won't work” during generation, the flow stops — and from then on, people only discuss what was said before that phrase.
fields.checkQuestion: Why can a strong expert in the room reduce the number of ideas?
fields.blocks/0/text: The same question about a good idea, but about **how to do it together without losing half the options.**
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** The meeting turns into an argument. Not the best idea wins, but the most insistent or senior person — and everyone else stops proposing.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Four rules, each against a specific loss mechanism
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Silently and in writing first.** Everyone writes on their own for five minutes — otherwise the first spoken idea anchors everyone.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Divergence and convergence separately.** First only collect, then only evaluate. Not simultaneously.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Quantity over quality.** The goal of the first stage is the number of options, not defending them.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Anonymous ideas.** Then people discuss the idea, not the person.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: A way to structure discussion by roles, not by people
fields.blocks/3/items/0: The entire group looks from one perspective at the same time: only facts, only risks, only benefits, only ideas.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: The point is that **no one is assigned the role of skeptic**: everyone criticizes, and all at the same time.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: It saves relationships rather than time: an objection stops being a personal stance.
fields.blocks/4/text: When there is someone in the group who “knows exactly how to do it”, others filter out their options in advance. A written first stage fixes this.
fields.blocks/4/title: An expert in the room reduces the number of ideas
fields.blocks/5/text:
First: discussed out loud. In an hour — six ideas, four of them proposed by the lead developer. They took his first one.

Second: five minutes silently and in writing, then gathered on a board without names. In the same hour — 23 ideas. Two of them no one would have said out loud because they sounded naive: “give the first book in full” and “remove registration before the first page”.

The second of those later produced the best result of the quarter.
fields.blocks/5/title: Vetka: two meetings about the same thing
fields.blocks/6/text: A group is good for quantity and bad for decision-making: one person should make the choice in the end, otherwise a compromise wins that satisfies everyone and works for no one. And unconstrained generation produces ideas unrelated to the task — you set the frame before the meeting.
